---
title: "loss functions"
---

## the big picture

- loss, likelihood, log-likelihood, and deviance are four ways of answering the same question — how bad is my model? — from different angles.

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| term | used in | idea |
|---|---|---|
| loss function | ml (general) | what we minimise |
| likelihood | statistics | how probable the observed data is under the model |
| log-likelihood | statistics | the same thing, with easier math |
| deviance | glms (e.g. logistic regression) | "badness" relative to a perfect model |

:::

## loss functions

- a loss function measures prediction error; training minimises it.
- linear regression typically minimises squared error loss: $\text{loss}=\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2$.
- logistic regression minimises log loss (cross-entropy); see [evaluation metrics](evaluation-metrics.qmd) for its formula and when to use it.

## likelihood & log-likelihood

- the statistics framing flips the question: how likely is the data I observed, given this model? $L(\theta)=P(\text{data}\mid\theta)$.
- high likelihood means a good model; low likelihood means a bad one. fitting a model this way means maximising likelihood, not minimising error.
- taking the log turns products into sums and makes derivatives easier: $\log L(\theta)$. maximising log-likelihood gives the same optimum as maximising likelihood, since log is monotonic.

## the key connection

- minimising loss and maximising log-likelihood are the same optimisation in disguise: $\{\text{minimise loss}\}=\{\text{maximise log-likelihood}\}$.
- example — linear regression: if the errors are gaussian, maximising the log-likelihood is algebraically equivalent to minimising the sum of squared errors. that's why ordinary least squares is also the maximum-likelihood estimator under gaussian noise.

## deviance

- deviance measures how far a model is from a perfect ("saturated") model — one that predicts every data point exactly: $\text{deviance}=2\big(\log L_{\text{perfect}}-\log L_{\text{model}}\big)$.
- a perfect model has deviance 0; a worse model has larger deviance, so lower deviance means a better fit.
- for many models, deviance is just a scaled version of the loss:

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| model | loss | deviance |
|---|---|---|
| linear regression | squared error loss (rss) | rss itself — equals $-$log-likelihood up to a constant |
| logistic regression | log loss (cross-entropy) | $2\times$ log loss |

:::

## practical considerations

- "minimise the loss," "maximise the likelihood," and "minimise the deviance" are, for most standard models, three descriptions of the same fitting procedure — expect to see all three depending on whether a source comes from an ml or a statistics background.
- which loss to pick depends on the outcome type and what errors should cost: squared error for continuous outcomes assuming roughly gaussian noise, log loss for probabilistic binary/multiclass outcomes, and task-specific losses (hinge loss for margin-based classifiers, pseudo-residuals from the loss gradient in gradient boosting) elsewhere in these notes.
- a non-convex loss surface (e.g. in neural networks) means gradient descent can only be guaranteed to find a local, not global, minimum — see [gradient descent](gradient-descent.qmd).
